items.title: Who Sat for Jan van Eyck’s Arnolfini Portrait? A New Catalog Essay Suggests It May Have Been the Artist
items.summary:
The catalog for the exhibition “Van Eyck: The Portraits” opening at London’s National Gallery on November 21, has reignited a long-standing debate about the identity of couple in the Early Netherlandish master’s mysterious Arnolfini Portrait (1434). As reported in the Art Newspaper , one of the catalog’s essays suggests that the man in the painting, usually identified as a member of the Arnolfini family of Italian merchants, is in fact Jan van Eyck himself.

In the painting, which is owned by the National Gallery and a centerpiece of the show, an elegantly dressed man and woman pose hand in hand in a private room. Every item in the chamber, including the couple’s fur-trimmed clothing, the oriental carpet on the floor, and even the orange resting on a windowsill—an expensive luxury at the time—signals understated wealth.

The man and the woman are clearly husband and wife, though the work does not, as was once believed, depict a marriage ceremony. A 16th-century inventory of the holdings of Margaret of Austria, the painting’s owner at the time, identifies it as “Hernoul le Fin” or “Arnoult Fin,” which is widely interpreted by art historians as “Arnolfini.”

Scholars have disagreed however, however, about which Arnolfini the man in the painting might be. Possible candidates are either Giovanni di Arrigo Arnolfini (though recent discoveries suggest he was not married at the time the painting was made), or more likely his cousin, Giovanni di Nicolao Arnolfini, who would have been in his late thirties in 1434.

Giovanni’s first wife Costanza Trenta died in 1433; thus, according…
items.t: Who Sat for Jan van Eyck’s Arnolfini Portrait? A New Catalog Essay Suggests It May Have Been the Artist

items.title: Why Is the Whitney Museum Selling a De Kooning Painting?
items.summary:
Willem de Kooning, “Yellow River” (1958) (image courtesy Christie’s Images Ltd. 2026) Looking to cash in on marquee week in New York, the Whitney Museum of American Art has consigned a Willem de Kooning painting from its collection to Christie's for its 20th-century evening sale tomorrow, November 17. Once a promised gift to the museum, de Kooning's “Yellow River” (1958) is expected to fetch up to $18 million. 

The practice of museum deaccessioning has long been a subject of controversy . In 2022, the Association of Art Museum Directors (AAMD) loosened its policy to allow institutions to apply funds from the sale of deaccessioned art toward the “direct care” of their collections. 

A lot description for “Yellow River” on Christie's website notes that the proceeds will benefit the Whitney's collection. The Whitney has not yet responded to Hyperallergic 's request for comment, but a museum spokesperson told Artnet News that deaccessioning is “a component of the Whitney’s collections strategic plan, allowing the museum to thoughtfully evaluate and refine its holdings in support of its long-term collection priorities.”

The de Kooning painting going under that hammer had a rooted connection to the Whitney before it was bequeathed to the museum in 2023. Postwar art collector, attorney, and museum trustee David Solinger, who would go on to become the museum's first president beyond the Whitney family in 1966, purchased the work from de Kooning's sold-out exhibition at Sidney Janis Gallery in 1959. 

“Yellow River” emerged from a series of “highway" paintings representing the…
items.t: Why Is the Whitney Museum Selling a De Kooning Painting?

items.title: Sotheby’s Hospices de Beaune Charity Wine Sale Nets $15.8 M. in France, with One Barrel Selling for Record $1.1 M.
items.summary:
The annual Hospices de Beaune charity wine auction in Burgundy, France, organized by Sotheby’s, generated €14.4 million ($15.8 million) on Sunday. It was the 166th edition of the the historic sale, and its top lot—known as the “Presidents’ Barrel”—was bought by Brazilian wine merchant Aloar Pereira Linoa for €770,000 ($848,732) in the room. 

Just after the hammer came down, there was a surprise twist; the Faiveley family, one of Bergundy’s most important wine-making dynasties, pledged another €230,000 ($251,000), rounding up the total to a cool €1 million ($1.1 million).

The donation brought the charitable total to a new record. Proceeds from the 228-liter Presidents’ Barrel (exempt from Sotheby’s buyer’s premium fees), which holds a Clos de Vougeot Grand Cru, will go to ARSLA and DEBRA, two charities supporting people with rare diseases. They are charcot disease and epidermolysis bullosa, otherwise known as “butterfly skin disease.”

Each year, celebrities are enlisted to rev up the crowd and encourage bidding on the main barrel. This year saw comedy duo Éric Judor and Ramzy Bedia, alongside actress Aurelie Vandevoorde, temporarily take over at the rostrum. At one point, Judor promised the next bidder a minor role in his new movie, as the French trio had the room in raptures during the 18-minute bidding battle. “All you New Yorkers here… you’re willing to pay $20 for a hotdog but you won’t pay for this wine?” he joked.

I’ve never seen people singing at an auction before, but at one point the entire crowd erupted into a standing performance of “Ban Bourguignon,”…
items.t: Sotheby’s Hospices de Beaune Charity Wine Sale Nets $15.8 M. in France, with One Barrel Selling for Record $1.1 M.

items.title: Talking Art and Data With Mona Chalabi
items.summary:
Mona Chalabi is a Pulitzer Prize-winning journalist, and as much as it shows across her incredible body of visual data reporting, she has always kept her eye on another prize entirely. I sat down with her earlier this fall at Christopher Park across from the Stonewall Inn, a site of protest and resistance, to talk about her new book and her career as a whole.

The culmination of six years of research, interviews, and illustration, Ten Lives breaks the silence around class in her characteristic visual style. To me, it’s a reflection of her principled approach to journalism and storytelling that feel utterly lost in a world where self-promotion, access, and branding can matter more than the work itself. Chalabi brings a refreshing integrity and playful approach to reporting unflinchingly on the genocide in Palestine, the horrors of the healthcare system, and massive wealth inequality. While she insists her work isn’t “fine art,” it’s perhaps the purest example of what art should do: challenge our ways of seeing. She’s also uncommonly funny, humble, and perceptive. (Can you tell I’m a fan?)

Class is also at the center of photographer Mark Alice Durant’s memoiristic book, which critic Melissa Holbrook Pierson likens to Rainer Maria Rilke’s Letters to a Young Poet for our dystopian world of 2026. Other books in this edition similarly respond to the Orwellian state of art and power. Nitasha Dhillon and Amin Husain, both scholars and activists, have organized protests against the Museum of Modern Art in 2021, the Whitney Biennial in 2019, and the Guggenheim Abu Dhabi in 2015,…
items.t: Talking Art and Data With Mona Chalabi

items.title: What Mary Lovelace O'Neal Left Behind
items.summary:
Upon her death in May 2026, the abstract painter Mary Lovelace O’Neal left behind a monumental body of work. Her oeuvre includes signature large blackened canvases, marked by fluid, ecstatic gestures in neon paint that resemble the glowing afterimages of a moving flame. O’Neal’s first posthumous exhibition, Requiem, is a fitting self-elegy for the painter precisely because nothing about it feels mournful. 

The work could not be more vital, and in it one feels the artist’s energetic and intuitive handling of paint as a kind of physical charge. O’Neal’s compositions transmit a powerful sense of presence and force, as though inviting viewers into the vicarious experience of an artist grappling with the formal concerns of color and line before transcending them. 

The result is an almost oceanic feeling, one I imagine is equally profound in the making of a painting as staggering as the intense, cascading standout “Requiem for a Daffodil” (1997). The black, fingerlike marks that protrude from the surrounding deep navy seem to be reaching for the floral clusters and reeds in the painting’s top half, like a perpetual grasping at splendor in the shadows. 

Though non-representational, these works continually approach figuration, filled with partial outlines of human and animal forms. These half-figures peer through their dark surroundings, like the pink mass in the center of “What’s Time to a Pig” (c. 1990s), and are caught in a constant state of emergence. Like an act of divine creation, O’Neal captures the transformation of raw material into something seemingly miraculous…
items.t: What Mary Lovelace O'Neal Left Behind

items.title: Latinx Artists Are the New Visionaries
items.summary:
Latinx communities are facing one of the most aggressive series of attacks in recent history, with many families enduring the pain of separation, persecution, and dehumanization. But if you’ve been paying attention to Latinx arts and culture, you’ll see that as we are being told to hide and disappear, artists are stepping into newfound confidence, showcasing the full value and complexity of our identities. The work of these new visionaries is a rallying cry: Now is the time to write, create, and make art boldly — together.

Over the past several years, I have documented the work of Latinx creatives across public art, fashion, and independent filmmaking, and I believe we have every reason to feel unabashedly optimistic. Across these fields, artists are choosing to create work that is deeply rooted in their communities, drawing directly from vernacular traditions, oral histories, and family memories that were once pushed to the margins. They are using culture to reclaim heritage and reframe the narrative. This marks a distinct departure from older paradigms, where artists were taught — or forced — to believe that conforming to mainstream, assimilationist models was the only path to success. While they recognize there are no guarantees of commercial or institutional rewards, their work stems from a shared conviction: We have rich cultures to offer, and we will tell our stories by any means necessary.

Sometimes, their methods involve elevating vernacular and popular culture to expand traditional aesthetic repertoires. We see this in contemporary fashion with designers like…
items.t: Latinx Artists Are the New Visionaries

items.title: Arta Moves Beyond Shipping Art, to Helping Collectors Pay for It
items.summary:
For years, Arta has helped collectors get art from a gallery or an auction house to their homes. Now, it wants to help them pay for it, too.

The New York–based technology company has launched Arta Pay, a new financing service that allows collectors to buy art, watches, jewelry, and other luxury goods on credit, paying for them over 10 months while sellers receive the full purchase price within days.

The service offers credit lines ranging from $1,000 to more than $100,000, targeting a part of the market that has often fallen between conventional consumer financing and the large art loans offered by private banks.

Here’s how it works: A collector buying a $10,000 painting would put down at least 10 percent, or $1,000, and pay the remaining balance in nine monthly installments. There’s a flat financing charge of 12.5 percent on the amount borrowed, disclosed upfront. In this example, that would add $1,125 to the cost of the painting if the buyer takes the full nine months to repay it.

The gallery, meanwhile, gets its $10,000 within five business days, without having to worry about collecting the remaining payments. Arta takes on the repayment and fraud risk, and charges sellers no processing fees.

“We’ve spent years building the post-purchase technology that powers commerce across art, luxury, and collectibles,” Adam Fields, Arta’s founder and CEO, said. The new service, he added, is designed to make the transactions easier.

Arta has become a familiar name behind the scenes of the art market, providing shipping, insurance, and other logistical services to auction…
items.t: Arta Moves Beyond Shipping Art, to Helping Collectors Pay for It

items.title: What Does Frida Kahlo Mean Today?
items.summary:
These days, Frida Kahlo isn’t free. She is the plastic cosmetic bag in an Ulta carousel. She is a throw pillow in a World Market bin. Her name and image might be the most commodified of the 20th century, so ubiquitous that she feels emptied of meaning. Or is she?

Relying primarily on the testimony of Mexican voices, Frida: The Girl That Just Doesn’t Go Away , a new documentary by Trisha Ziff, poses this question across a colorful spectrum of socio-cultural contexts, steering clear of whitewashing the artist’s personal history. “I learned about Communism from Frida’s bookshelf,” shares actress and activist Ofelia Medina, who visited Kahlo’s home on a sixth-grade field trip. 

Film still of Frida: The Girl That Just Doesn’t Go Away (2026), directed by Trisha Ziff “Frida gave me strength, she gave me a life and a job,” explains Juana López Sánchez, an Indigenous artisan whose livelihood is selling hand-crafted Frida dolls in Mexico City.
items.t: What Does Frida Kahlo Mean Today?

items.title: Video Artist Pipilotti Rist Wins MIT’s $100,000 Arts Award
items.summary:
Pipilotti Rist, one of the most widely acclaimed living video artists, has another feather in her cap in the form of next year’s Eugene McDermott Award in the Arts, a prize given out by the Massachusetts Institute of Technology that comes with $100,000 and a residency on campus.

The Swiss artist is known for phantasmagoric installations that have harnessed video technology to explore the human body in all its many forms. Often working with a heavy dose of humor, Rist has thoughtfully used her camera to explore sexuality, sleep states, and the female form.

Today, she is perhaps best known for her 1997 video installation Ever Is Over All , in which a woman walks down a city street and smashes in car windows with flowers. The work was memorably retooled in the visual album for Beyoncé’s Lemonade .

“I am kissing your Institute and your feet,” Rist said in a statement about the MIT award. “I am immensely touched and grateful to have this trust and investment in ideas I’ve yet to conceive. I’m honored to receive an award that has been granted to so many of my heroes, and look forward to collaborating closely with the brilliant minds at MIT.”

Her past achievements include representing Switzerland at the Venice Biennale in 2005 and a retrospective that appeared at New York’s New Museum in 2016. According to the website for Hauser & Wirth, the mega-gallery that represents her alongside New York’s Luhring Augustine, Rist will stage a permanent installation at the long-awaited Guggenheim Abu Dhabi when it opens in December.
items.t: Video Artist Pipilotti Rist Wins MIT’s $100,000 Arts Award

items.title: TEFAF Maastricht Names 277 Exhibitors for 2027 Fair
items.summary:
TEFAF Maastricht, the European Fine Art Foundation’s Dutch art fair, has lined up 277 international galleries for its 2027 edition at MECC, a convention center just outside the center of town, and the fair’s longtime home. TEFAF also runs a New York edition, at the Park Avenue Armory, since 2016.)

TEFAF is known for its rigorous vetting process, massive floral displays, and high-profile museum buyers, not to mention top-notch examples from 7,000 years’ worth of art history. Dealers at last year’s fair were “more than pleased” with sales and attendance, ARTnews reported.

Newcomers to the 2027 edition’s main section include Galerie AB and Galerie Édouard Ambroselli, (France); Gallery Arte y Ritual (Spain); Galerie Bei Der Albertina (Austria); Butchoff Antiques (UK); Hazlitt (UK and US); Xavier Hufkens (Belgium); Thomsen Gallery and Martos Gallery (US); and Thaddaeus Ropac (UK, France, Austria, Italy, South Korea).

The fair will once again include two special sections: Showcase, featuring nine emerging dealers, all showing at TEFAF for the first time, and Focus, dedicated to seven galleries with booths that zero in on a single artist or curatorial concept. Three of this year’s Focus galleries are new to the fair: Daguet-Bresson from France, Edel Assanti from the UK, and Repetto Gallery from Switzerland.

items.title: Martin Puryear’s Liberatory Violence
items.summary:
ATLANTA — Despite my best efforts to be anything else, I am a writer, and not even the Marines-like insanity of Bard’s interdisciplinary MFA or my day job in the library could erase that from me. Every object instantly becomes a word I see on a perfectly white page, a symbol made up of assorted shapes like “bicycle” (object that carried me from my home to the High Museum of Art) or “press pass” (object that allows me into the High Museum of Art), a compulsion that is always at its worst when viewing sculpture in the page-white tomb of a museum.

I was grateful for that compulsion, however, when I viewed Martin Puryear’s Nexus . Writing, underneath its surface, is extremely violent, exceptionally bloody, and annihilatory in scope. It is almost impossible to describe the reality of this fact on the page, and I have struggled even further to articulate this vocally to others, even other writers. So when walking into Nexus and “Bask” (1976) was there, lying as still and deadly as a knife on its white plinth, I smiled in surprised relief and my body physically relaxed. Puryear is noted for his use of natural materials — wood, rawhide, fiber — and his attention to traditional practices like basket weaving, boatmaking, tanning, and structure building from peoples around the world, which obscures the sculptures’ violence under that tricky word, “natural.”

Installation view of Martin Puryear: Nexus with "Bask" (1976), stained pine, in the foreground
items.t: Martin Puryear’s Liberatory Violence

items.title: Restitution Claim on $180M Van Gogh Shakes Up Sotheby's Marquee Week
items.summary:
Heirs of a prominent Jewish publishing family have called on Sotheby's to withdraw a rare Vincent van Gogh painting highlighted in the marquee auction sales in New York City this week, claiming that the work had been sold under duress amid Nazi persecution in Europe. 

The heirs allege that the family member who owned the painting, which Sotheby's valued at a record-breaking $180 million, sold it because of Nazi-imposed restrictions on what emigrant Jews were allowed to take with them at the time. 

Sotheby's confirmed to Hyperallergic that the painting is still slated to go under the hammer this Wednesday, November 18, and that it was aware of the heirs' concerns and “takes provenance and restitution matters extremely seriously and has undertaken extensive research into the [painting's] ownership history.”
items.t: Restitution Claim on $180M Van Gogh Shakes Up Sotheby's Marquee Week

items.title: Vienna Museum’s Mummified Remains Reveal Cats Lived and Died Brutally in Ancient Egypt
items.summary:
Cats in ancient Egypt may have endured nine exceptionally hard lives, according to findings related to feline skulls in the collection of the Natural History Museum in Vienna.

As reported by Popular Mechanics , research on 131 skulls from a funerary site in Middle Egypt led by zooarchaeologist Wim Van Neer of the Royal Belgian Institute of Natural Sciences revealed “disturbing” evidence that the cats may have been killed for the sake of offerings to the goddess known as Bastet. “Fourteen of the skulls show traumatic injuries, including blunt-force and sharp-force trauma,” the report reads. “Beyond fight wounds, some injuries were inflicted long enough before death to show signs of healing, which suggests that the animals may have endured physical violence from humans while still alive.”

It gets worse: “The cats’ treatment before death also seems to have been deplorable. Although no ancient records describe how the cats were kept, the researchers inferred that they were probably held in crowded enclosures. This could explain the fights, as well as the attacks on domestic cats by jungle cats, which were caught in marshlands or along the banks of the Nile when Egypt was lusher than it is today.”

The research, published in the Journal of Archaeological Science , also shared grim news regarding the manner in which the killed cats met their ends. “Skull fractures were the most common cause of death, whereas evidence of strangulation occurred less frequently,” the researchers said. “Our observations of traumatic lesions on the skulls provide evidence of fatal injuries, as well…
items.t: Vienna Museum’s Mummified Remains Reveal Cats Lived and Died Brutally in Ancient Egypt

items.title: Volcanoes! Floods! The Apocalypse! All Appear in a Rare $1.3 M. German Manuscript Coming to Christie’s
items.summary:
Natural disasters, cosmic phenomena, and Biblical tales of destruction have long fascinated humankind and sometimes have been thought to convey messages from above. Christie’s London will offer a prominent example of a 16th-century German manuscript with 167 miniature renditions of phenomena such as comets, monsters, and the end of the world.

In the The Book of Miracles , also known as the Augsburger Wunderzeichenbuch , which bears an estimate of £700,000–£1 million (about $923,000–$1.3 million), readers see bloodred moons, fiery comets, floods, cities smashed by earthquakes, swarms of giant locusts, volcanic eruptions, dragons, and “monstrous births.” It comes to the auction block as part of Christie’s classic week sale of valuable books and manuscripts in London on December 10. The house bills it as “one of the most remarkable surviving picture chronicles” of its century.

The volume comes from the holdings of the widely respected American collector Mickey Cartin. Christie’s is offering up to $8 million worth of selections from his collection, ranging from Netherlandish painting to contemporary art and, of course, rare books. Upward of 80 objects will be spread over more than 10 auctions in London, Paris, and New York, from this November until July 2027.

The Book of Miracles was completed in the city of Augsburg around 1552. Its geographical origins are known because some of the captions refer to events “here in Augsburg,” and the paper bears watermarks associated with that city and time period. The makers are thought to be Hans Burgkmair the Younger, Heinrich Vogtherr…
items.t: Volcanoes! Floods! The Apocalypse! All Appear in a Rare $1.3 M. German Manuscript Coming to Christie’s

items.title: “Mighty Miniatures” Features Over 300 Tiny Artworks From Indigenous Communities Across the Western Hemisphere
items.summary:
“ Mighty Miniatures ,” an exhibition celebrating the intricate art of miniatures, is on view at the Smithsonian’s National Museum of the American Indian in New York from Saturday, November 21 through Friday, August 20, 2027. Curated by Anya Montiel (Tohono O’odham descent), the exhibition features over 300 pieces of art that showcase the skill of Indigenous weavers, sculptors, carvers and other artists that work on a miniscule scale.

The exhibition includes tiny masterpieces created over a span of nearly two centuries by artists from Indigenous communities from North and South America, as well as Hawai'i and the Caribbean. The small works reflect worldviews and cultural expressions, encouraging play and transferring intergenerational knowledge. 

“‘Mighty Miniatures’   brings together some of the smallest works in the museum collection, reaching across the Western Hemisphere and spanning nearly 200 years,” Montiel said. “It is amazing to see how these miniatures have been made with such skill, ingenuity, and detail. This exhibition is a celebration of Indigenous artistry on a small scale and the artists who create them.”

items.t: “Mighty Miniatures” Features Over 300 Tiny Artworks From Indigenous Communities Across the Western Hemisphere

items.title: British Museums Are Experiencing a ‘Bayeux Bounce’ in Attendance, Thanks to Replicas of the Tapestry
items.summary:
The Bayeux Tapestry is the gift that keeps on giving. UK museums such as Reading Museum and the Great North Museum: Hancock are experiencing a “Bayeux bounce,” according to the Museums Association .

Replicas of the scroll-like panel of linen cloth, which measures at 230 feet long and is populated with 58 scenes, are driving visitors to museums other than the British Museum, where the tapestry is on loan until July next year. Tickets to the British Museum’s presentation have been sold out numerous times.

Reading Museum’s museum manager, Matthew Williams, said that the museum’s Victorian replica of the Bayeux Tapestry has driven a 74 percent increase in footfall since October, with 16,693 visitors. The tapestry at Reading Museum is free to visit, and photography is allowed, unlike at the British Museum, where the tapestry is ticketed at £33 and photography is banned in order to control the long queues.

“We have trained more staff to deliver our public tours and recruited more welcome volunteers to help us manage the crowds, especially at weekends and school holidays,” said Williams. “We have made sure to keep our website updated to manage expectations and to clearly show when the [replica] Bayeux Tapestry is closed for booked tours or when it will be busy, to avoid disappointment.” 

The Bayeux Tapestry replica has resulted in optimistic numbers for the museum, with tours booked until June 2027, the cafe’s income up by 46 percent, donations increased by 83 percent, and shop sales soaring by 93 percent.

The copy of the Bayeux Tapestry at the Great North Museum: Hancock is…
items.t: British Museums Are Experiencing a ‘Bayeux Bounce’ in Attendance, Thanks to Replicas of the Tapestry

items.title: Tate Turns Julio Le Parc Into Instagram Art
items.summary:
LONDON — In Paris, in the years leading up to the massive social upheavals of 1968, Julio Le Parc was making the first of his Game Rooms . These were collections of works that aimed to playfully destabilize the viewer’s experience, such as seats with springs that challenged the act of sitting, areas of uneven tile floors, and patterned discs designed to be manually spun. But for Le Parc, as well as the progressive collective Groupe de Recherche d’Art Visuel (GRAV) that he co-founded, the works were about far more than entertainment. Indeed, he hoped that cultivating the audience’s active participation would not only disrupt what he saw as the hierarchical and passive nature of the museum, but also effect a political awakening outside of it.

A recreation of one of the Game Rooms appears in the exhibition Julio Le Parc: Light. Colour. Action. , which was “developed in close dialogue with the artist,” before his death earlier this year at the age of 97. Though the current world, as in 1960s Paris, grapples with mounting social and political tensions, one is unlikely to describe today’s art museum experience as “passive.” Indeed, outgoing Tate Modern Interim Director Catherine Wood notes in the exhibition catalog’s foreword, “At a time of heightened popularity for exhibitions touting immersive and interactive experiences, celebrating Julio Le Parc’s seven-decade career with a monographic exhibition at Tate Modern feels especially meaningful and urgent.” 

Installation view of Julio Le Parc: Lights. Colour. Action.
items.t: Tate Turns Julio Le Parc Into Instagram Art

items.title: After Exile, Luis Manuel Otero Alcántara’s Prison Drawings Arrive in New York
items.summary:
In one of Luis Manuel Otero Alcántara’s prison drawings, swans skim a swimming pool inside a cell. In another, a clownish figure peers over the prison wall, perched with apparent ease on barbed wire. The Cuban artist and leader of the San Isidro Movement made thousands of such works in Guanajay, a maximum-security prison outside Havana, where he served time after his arrest on July 11, 2021, amid anti-government protests across the island. His release this year, after international outcry over creative freedom, was contingent on exile to the United States. A small selection of those works makes up “Tocar el cielo,” their first public showing, now at the New York gallery Foreign & Domestic (curated by Alexander Meurice, and on view through December 13).

Art that emerges from incarceration tends to speak first in material, with scarcity making resourcefulness something like a protagonist. Otero Alcántara recounted drawing on drink cartons and cigarette packs, and smuggling in colored ink that ended up on other prisoners’ skin, when bodies were canvas enough. Who gets to make art inside, and who can get supplies to them, comes with its own politics. But he describes his five years in prison as one long performance, an “involuntary artistic gesture,” and the show reflects rather than transcribes the specifics of injustice. It’s an oblique testimony to how, bereft of sky or savior, the mind can slip its confines.

ARTnews spoke with Otero Alcántara via email about his experience making art in prison, and settling into his second life in Miami. The following conversation has…
items.t: After Exile, Luis Manuel Otero Alcántara’s Prison Drawings Arrive in New York

items.title: Curator Christiane Paul Helped Write the History of Net Art. She’s Doing It Again with a New Survey at the Whitney.
items.summary:
Editor’s Note: This story is part of Newsmakers , a new ARTnews series where we interview the movers and shakers who are making change in the art world. 

Rare are the times when a New York museum has turned over an entire floor to a presentation of digital art. That makes “artport: A History of Internet Art,” opening at the Whitney Museum on Saturday, an outlier in the institution’s programming—and something of a major occasion.

The titular artport is an online gallery launched in 2001 by curator Christiane Paul, who has since gone on to commission plenty of works in the intervening 25 years, by artists ranging from JODI to Mimi Ọnụọha. Officially indexed as part of the Whitney collection since 2015, artport continues to commission artists. The most recent was Jazsalyn, who, for one work staged earlier this year, proposed what she called “Black Metatheories” as means of forming something alternative to AI and called on users to respond to a range of prompts, including one that reads: “Consider blackness. How does life persist within the spectrum of impossible possibility?”

Artport’s offerings live on the Whitney’s website. Generally, however, they have not been show in the Whitney’s galleries, something that will change with Paul’s exhibition opening this week, which features more than works associated with artport. The show is yet another digital art–focused exhibition from one of the great thinkers on the subject. She literally wrote the book on digital art in 2003, and is currently in the process of writing a follow-up to it.

ARTnews spoke with Paul, a curator of…
items.t: Curator Christiane Paul Helped Write the History of Net Art. She’s Doing It Again with a New Survey at the Whitney.

items.title: Draconian Trump Executive Order Could Strip Art Orgs of Nonprofit Status
items.summary:
After the Wall Street Journal reported earlier this month that the White House is considering an executive order that would strip nonprofits deemed to have alleged "terrorist ties" of their tax-exempt status, many arts and culture organizations are bracing for what could be a series of politically targeted attacks from the Trump administration. 

According to the report, officials are reviewing Section 501(p)(2)(C) of the United States Internal Revenue Code, which authorizes the president to label nonprofits that are allegedly "supporting or engaging in terrorist activity." Organizations tagged with the label would have their tax-exempt status immediately suspended, spelling a potentially devastating blow to their operations. 

The White House has not made an official confirmation or announcement of the measure, with a spokesperson telling Hyperallergic that "any policy announcements will come directly from the President," and "discussions about potential decisions or their impacts are otherwise baseless speculation."
items.t: Draconian Trump Executive Order Could Strip Art Orgs of Nonprofit Status

items.title: Advance Your Creative Practice With a Graduate Degree From the University of Louisville
items.summary:
With substantial scholarships, exceptional facilities, accomplished faculty, and private studios, students pursuing an  MFA in Studio Art and Design  at the University of Louisville have the resources and creative freedom to develop their artistic practice within a dynamic, supportive community.

The rigorous 60-credit MFA program encourages experimentation, critical inquiry, and interdisciplinary exploration. Students may pursue interdisciplinary practices or concentrate on individual media, including ceramics, drawing, glass, painting, photography, printmaking, sculpture, design, new media, and installation.

Located in Louisville's Portland arts district, the MFA program occupies a dedicated, newly renovated warehouse featuring individual graduate studios, state-of-the-art production facilities, laboratories, a seminar room, and an exhibition gallery. This distinctive environment provides students with the space, resources, and opportunities to develop ambitious creative projects.

The Hite Institute also offers a 31-credit-hour  MA in Art History or Curatorial Studies . Combining critical theory, art historical research, contemporary art, and hands-on exhibition experience, the program prepares students for careers in museums, galleries, curatorial practice, arts administration, and art writing, as well as further academic study.

Founded in 1946, the endowed Hite Institute of Art + Design has built a distinctive identity grounded in its avant-garde origins and oriented to creative experimentation and critical inquiry. Its accomplished faculty of practicing artists,…

Last week, a survey conducted by Critical Minded and the Rabkin Foundation quantified the precarity of independent US-based art magazines amid a climate of censorship, corporate takeovers, and economic instability. It’s no wonder, when media companies decide to partner with Amazon on art initiatives (cough, cough, Penske). Senior Editor Valentina Di Liscia breaks down the survey results and what they can teach us about the future of independent, critical arts journalism.

Speaking of which, Staff Writer Anna Lee reports on a coalition of Tribal Nations opposing a bill that would threaten Native sites if Congress passes it. Longtime Angeleno Matt Stromberg considers an engrossing if occasionally overwrought book by James Cahill that explores the influential friendship between David Hockney and Betty Freeman, the arts patron at the center of one of his most recognizable paintings. And if that isn’t enough, Aaron Short shares a wry dispatch from the preview of the Art Dealers Association of America’s art fair in New York City — the tickets may have been $250 a pop, but at least there were unlimited dumplings and champagne to sweeten the deal?

items.title: Tamsin Greig is sensational in a Cranford where comedy and pain are in perfect balance
items.summary:
Orange Tree theatre, London
This streamlined adaptation of Elizabeth Gaskell’s novel gets right to the heart of her characters, who face heartbreak and loss but gain from the strength of female friendship

There’s more than one worry for any new dramatisation of Elizabeth Gaskell’s novel to contend with. There is the risk of this story, set among the unmarried women and widows of a fictional English town, being considered Middlemarch lite – and overshadowed by the Royal Shakespeare Company’s luminous adaptation of the George Eliot novel, currently running in Stratford-Upon-Avon. Then there is the 2007 BBC adaptation of Cranford, which threw every national treasure at it, trowelling on the lovable humour and sentiment as it did so.

This production, however, co-created by Lin Coghlan, Shaun McKenna and Josh Roche, bypasses all those dangers by leaning into theatricality – and sheer good acting. The script is by Coghlan and McKenna, who previously adapted The Forsyte Saga, staged last year by the RSC. They confidently fillet the original and also add their own little inventions.

items.title: Special Edition: Jesus
items.summary:
Framed by their car’s windshield, and then again by my rearview mirror, a man and a woman who seem to be a couple look like they'd rather be anywhere but together. He’s behind the wheel, doing all the talking; she’s looking straight ahead, motionless like a marble statue. Gradually, her face wears a desperate expression that only grows more hopeless as he continues talking and gesticulating.  

In the supermarket checkout line, I pick up a copy of TIME magazine for the first time in God knows how long, drawn to a painting of Jesus Christ on the cover. It’s a special edition promising to tell us “Who he was. Who he is. His miracles, his mission, his love.” I expect to see a lot of biblical sheep inside, but I don’t find any. I buy the issue as an artifact. I stopped believing in TIME magazine a long time ago. 

Down the street, a place that pretended to be a legitimate art gallery for a couple of months, showing the worst possible commercial art, has finally given up, and now it’s selling fur coats. A man in a cowboy hat walks past two girls dancing for a social media video. The air is chilly, and I think of buying myself a leather jacket.    

And then I see her. 

She looks at me with the most loving eyes as she holds a stack of perfectly folded laundry. She comforts me with her wide, auspicious smile, her jet-black hair, and her wrinkle-free, porcelain skin. I feel safe, accepted, and not judged. “Fast service, same day,” she promises because she’s just a model in an ad for a laundromat. 

—Hakim Bishara, editor-in-chief

items.title: 45% of US Independent Arts Publications Face Existential Crisis, Report Finds
items.summary:
A new report tracks the challenges facing publications that cover arts and culture. (edit Valentina Di Liscia/ Hyperallergic, image KC Green) Nearly half of independent publications covering arts and culture in the United States said their business models will not be sustainable without “profound changes” to the current funding landscape, according to a report from Critical Minded and the Dorothea and Leo Rabkin Foundation released this week. 

The new survey notably identifies a disturbing correlation between censorship concerns, including external pressure from advertisers and sponsors, and financial precarity. The 41% of respondents who said they faced free-speech pressures or threats in the last two years were more likely to report funding declines, throwing into stark relief how what outlets choose to cover — or not — may determine whether they can pay staff and contributors, or keep the lights on altogether.

“Support for Arts and Culture Journalism: A Survey of Independent Publications in the United States” polled 141 independent outlets that cover the arts on issues impacting the field and strategies used to address them. The anonymized respondents are based in 34 states and the District of Columbia, with the highest concentration (38.2%) in the Northeast, and reach an average annual audience of about half a million.

items.title: Hamlet Hail to the Thief could have been rotten but redeems Radiohead’s ‘record that got away’ | Alexis Petridis
items.summary:
The band’s uneven 2003 album has been judiciously reworked to accompany a staging of Shakespeare’s tragedy with quite extraordinary results

According to the programme notes, Thom Yorke had serious reservations about director Christine Jones’ idea to stage a production of Hamlet featuring music from Radiohead’s 2003 album Hail to the Thief. Who can blame him? Many criticisms have been laid at Radiohead’s door but being hopelessly naff isn’t one of them, and, alas, naff is very much the adjective you’d apply to a lot of attempts to meld Shakespeare and rock music.

You’re often in the realm of high camp – portentous, Bard-quoting heavy metal lyrics; Return to the Forbidden Planet’s jokey blending of The Tempest with 50s rock’n’roll; 2015’s These Paper Bullets, which relocated Much Ado About Nothing to swinging London, complete with Beatle-y songs by Green Day’s Billie Joe Armstrong – or of buttock-clenching disasters like Catch My Soul, a 1971 rock adaptation of Othello which required Black American soul singer PP Arnold to star opposite impresario Jack Good, playing the title role in blackface.
